# The Museum of Unfinished Things

On the morning the museum received its first cloud, Mara was trying to repair the kettle.

The cloud arrived in a wooden crate marked THIS SIDE UP, although the delivery driver admitted that nobody at the depot had agreed which side that meant. He had brought it on a handcart, beneath a tarpaulin, and now stood in the museum doorway with his cap dripping rain onto the tiles.

“Signature,” he said.

“What is it?”

“According to the form, an atmospheric remainder.”

Mara looked past him at the weather. The street was full of atmospheric remainders. They ran down the windows and collected in the pothole outside the pharmacy.

“We didn’t order one.”

“Nobody orders anything anymore. They just inherit it.”

He held out the clipboard.

The museum occupied a former railway station at the edge of a town that no longer had trains. Its official name was the Municipal Repository of Incomplete Endeavors, but somebody had stolen enough brass letters from the sign to leave MUNICIPAL POSITORY, and the council had declined to fund replacements.

Inside were forty-three unfinished paintings, a bridge that had never reached its opposite bank, nine doctoral theses, a knitted sleeve, the blueprints for a machine intended to translate birdsong, and a wedding cake preserved beneath glass.

The wedding had happened. The marriage, according to the donor, had not.

Mara signed for the cloud.

***

Her predecessor had left three instructions in a notebook.

First: Do not finish anything.

Second: Keep accurate records.

Third: The north window sticks in damp weather. Lift before pushing.

Mara considered the third instruction the most useful.

She had taken the job because it included a small apartment upstairs and because, after eleven years of restoring furniture, she had developed a pain in her right wrist that made precise work difficult. The museum required very little precision. Mostly it required dusting around people’s intentions.

Visitors were rare. Schoolchildren came in November, when their teachers had exhausted the town’s other educational attractions. Occasionally someone arrived with a parcel and the expression of a person bringing an animal to the vet.

“Would you take this?” they asked.

Mara always asked what it was meant to become.

A symphony. A business. A better kind of umbrella.

Sometimes they knew everything about the intended result. Sometimes they had forgotten.

The museum did not accept ordinary broken things. A broken chair had once succeeded in being a chair. An unfinished chair remained in negotiation with the idea.

Mara liked the distinction, though she understood why the council struggled to put it on a tourism leaflet.

She set the kettle aside and opened the crate.

Inside, suspended above a shallow copper tray, was a cloud approximately the size of a sleeping sheep. It smelled faintly of hot pavement.

A folded note lay beneath it.

*This was supposed to be rain.*

***

The note was unsigned.

Mara searched the packing straw and found an address in a village thirty miles north, a railway ticket dated seventeen years earlier, and a photograph of a woman standing beside an orchard.

The woman held a hose. Behind her, the trees were white with blossom.

Mara entered the acquisition in the ledger.

**Object 718: Cloud. Intended function: precipitation. Reason for incompletion: unknown.**

She hesitated over the condition report, then wrote:

**Restless.**

Throughout the afternoon, the cloud shifted inside its crate. It flattened when buses passed. It rose into a narrow tower when someone rang the museum bell. Once, while Mara was eating a sandwich, it produced a small internal flash.

“Absolutely not,” she told it.

The flash did not recur.

At four o’clock, a boy named Ivo came in carrying a violin case. He was twelve and visited every Thursday while his grandmother attended an appointment across the square.

He had been bringing the violin for six months. Mara had never heard him play it.

“What’s that?”

“A cloud.”

“I know. Why’s it indoors?”

“It hasn’t finished being something.”

Ivo considered this explanation with the courtesy children sometimes extend to adults who appear to be doing their best.

“Maybe it’s finished being a cloud.”

“Apparently it was supposed to rain.”

“That’s what people always say about clouds.”

He put the violin case behind the desk and went to look at the bridge.

***

The bridge occupied the old waiting room.

It had been built at one-twentieth scale by an engineer who spent thirty-two years proposing a pedestrian crossing over the river. There were drawings, surveys, traffic assessments, revised surveys, and a correspondence with the council so extensive that it required its own cabinet.

The engineer died before construction began.

Two years later, the council installed stepping-stones.

Ivo liked to lie on the floor and look through the model’s arches. Mara suspected he was imagining water where the carpet lay.

“Have you ever finished anything?” he asked that afternoon.

“Lots of things.”

“What?”

“Tables. Cabinets. A very ugly chest of drawers.”

“Did finishing make it less ugly?”

“No. But it made the ugliness more permanent.”

He nodded.

From the entrance hall came a soft pattering sound.

They hurried back.

The copper tray was dry, but the cloud had shed a handful of tiny white pellets. Mara picked one up. It melted against her palm.

“Hail,” she said.

“Close enough.”

“Not according to the note.”

Ivo looked at her. “Who gets to decide?”

Before she could answer, his grandmother appeared at the door. She was a small woman with a magnificent purple coat.

“Come along,” she said. “The doctor has decided I should walk more.”

“Is that bad?”

“It’s inconvenient. I’ve spent seventy-eight years learning where to sit.”

After they left, Mara moved the cloud away from the wedding cake and placed a second tray beside the first.

***

The council letter arrived on Monday.

It explained, across three pages, that the museum’s operating costs were disproportionate to measurable public benefit. The building would be repurposed at the end of summer.

Mara read the phrase *repurposed* several times.

There was no mention of what would happen to the collection.

She telephoned the number at the bottom of the letter and spoke to a man who called the objects “legacy holdings.”

“Some of them are quite large,” she said.

“We anticipate a disposal process.”

“There’s a bridge.”

“Is it functional?”

“No.”

“Then that should simplify matters.”

After the call, Mara walked through the rooms.

The unfinished paintings leaned toward landscapes that would never receive their skies. A half-built mechanical fox watched from its shelf with one glass eye. In a case by the stairs lay a letter beginning, *I have tried several times to tell you*, followed by three inches of blank paper.

She had always assumed that saving these things was useful.

Now she wondered whether she had merely arranged a comfortable place for them to disappear slowly.

Upstairs, her own belongings fit into seven boxes, though she had never packed them. There were clothes, books, dishes, tools she no longer used, and a small walnut drawer she had begun making before her wrist grew bad.

It had no cabinet to belong to.

She went downstairs and placed the council letter in the ledger.

The cloud had turned the color of a bruised peach.

***

On Thursday, Ivo found her writing to the address from the crate.

“Who’s that for?”

“Whoever sent us the cloud.”

“What are you asking?”

“How to look after it.”

“Ask why they stopped.”

“Stopped what?”

“Trying to make it rain.”

Mara crossed out a sentence.

Ivo opened his violin case.

The instrument inside was ordinary except for a patch of lighter varnish near the chin rest. He lifted it carefully, tightened the bow, and stood beside the desk.

“I’m supposed to be learning a piece,” he said.

“All right.”

“It’s not ready.”

“All right.”

He played six notes. The seventh squeaked. He began again.

Mara returned to her letter, which seemed to make it easier for him. After several attempts, he reached a phrase that rose unexpectedly and then stopped.

“That’s as far as I know.”

“It’s a good place.”

“It isn’t the end.”

“I noticed.”

He lowered the violin.

“My teacher says I keep starting over because I like the beginning best.”

“Do you?”

“I like knowing what happens.”

Outside, a bus sighed at the stop where trains had once discharged passengers. The cloud stirred.

“Could I leave it here?” Ivo asked.

“The violin?”

“The piece. Until I learn the rest.”

“We don’t usually take performances.”

“You took a cloud.”

This was difficult to dispute.

Mara found a blank card and wrote:

**Object 719: A piece of music, currently arriving.**

Ivo read the label twice.

Then he asked her not to mention it to his grandmother.

***

The reply came in a green envelope.

The writer was named Ada Vale. She had once worked in agricultural engineering. During a drought, she had developed a device to gather moisture from the air and release it over small areas.

It had worked, in a limited sense.

*The difficulty was persuading the moisture to let go,* she wrote.

The orchard in the photograph belonged to her sister. By the time Ada produced the cloud, the trees had already died.

*I kept it because I thought I might still solve the problem. Then I kept it because I had kept it so long.*

There were practical instructions: avoid enclosed cupboards, loud machinery, and excessive heat.

At the bottom, Ada had added:

*It responds to music, though not predictably. Please don’t consider that an explanation.*

Mara read the letter beside the cloud.

“You’re late,” she told it.

The cloud drifted against the lip of its crate.

That evening she carried the walnut drawer downstairs. She placed it on the reception desk, opened her tool roll, and examined its joints.

Her wrist hurt before she had done anything.

She put the tools away.

Then she took them out again and sharpened a pencil.

On a sheet of paper she drew a cabinet large enough to hold the drawer. She disliked it immediately.

She drew another.

At midnight, she had six bad designs, a sore hand, and an appetite. She made toast beneath the kitchen grill, burned one corner, and ate it standing up.

***

Mara did not begin with a campaign.

She made a sign.

**THURSDAY EVENINGS: BRING SOMETHING YOU HAVE NOT FINISHED.**

Beneath that, in smaller letters:

**You may also come without it.**

The first evening, nobody arrived until seven twenty, when the woman from the pharmacy brought a jigsaw puzzle in a biscuit tin.

“There’s a piece missing,” she said.

“That might be a different category.”

“I haven’t looked under the sofa yet.”

Mara admitted her provisionally.

Next came a retired bus driver with three chapters of a detective novel. Then Ivo and his grandmother, who brought nothing and explained that she intended to finish other people’s biscuits.

They sat around the long table in the former parcel office.

Mara had expected conversation about projects. Instead they talked about heating bills, a dangerous junction, and whether the bakery had changed its flour.

The bus driver read two pages aloud.

In his novel, a woman discovered a body in a greenhouse. The pharmacist interrupted to ask why someone with a greenhouse would buy tomatoes in February.

“Because she’s about to discover a body,” he said.

“That doesn’t affect the planting schedule.”

He made a note.

Ivo played the beginning of his piece. This time he continued beyond the place where he usually stopped, moving slowly through several uncertain bars.

From the hall came a faint rumble.

Everyone listened.

“Plumbing,” Mara said.

It was easier than explaining.

By closing time, the pharmacist had assembled the border of her puzzle.

She left it on the table.

***

The evenings grew without becoming popular.

Eight people came, then fourteen, then nine. Someone repaired a radio. Someone unraveled a jumper she no longer wanted to finish. A young father spent forty minutes writing a job application while his daughter arranged wooden offcuts into a town.

Mara brought out the unfinished chair.

“Are we allowed to touch the exhibits?” the father asked.

“I’m reconsidering the policy.”

She found her predecessor’s notebook and reread the first instruction.

Do not finish anything.

Below it, in a different ink, he had written something she had overlooked:

*Unless there is a good reason.*

Mara laughed so loudly that everyone turned.

There were arguments. The bus driver disliked suggestions that his detective should have a mobile phone. A woman who brought a box of fabric objected when someone called it clutter. Two friends stopped attending after a disagreement that had nothing to do with the museum.

But things happened.

The radio spoke.

The chair acquired a seat.

The pharmacist found her missing puzzle piece inside a slipper and seemed almost disappointed.

Mara’s drawer remained on the desk. One evening, a carpenter examined her sketches.

“This one’s possible,” he said.

“It’s awkward.”

“So’s the alcove upstairs. Measure it.”

They discussed tools she could hold without hurting herself.

Meanwhile, visitors signed a petition against the closure. Mara delivered it to the council with attendance figures, photographs, and a proposed budget.

She omitted the cloud from the photographs.

Its legal status seemed uncertain.

***

Ada Vale came in August.

She arrived carrying a canvas bag and wearing shoes whitened by road dust. Mara recognized her from the photograph, though her hair had shortened and gone gray.

“I thought I ought to see where it ended up.”

The cloud was over the long table. They had finally coaxed it out of its crate by moving Ivo’s music stand a little farther away each Thursday.

Ada stood beneath it.

“Oh,” she said.

Mara left them alone and put the kettle on. A volunteer had replaced its switch in June.

That evening, Ivo played the whole piece.

He made mistakes. He frowned through a difficult passage and hurried near the end. His grandmother sat with her handbag clasped firmly on her knees.

On the final note, the cloud contracted.

A drop struck the table.

Then another.

“Paper,” Mara said, and everyone scrambled.

The detective novel was rescued. The job applications were lifted clear. Someone moved the radio. Rain fell steadily onto the empty biscuit plate.

Ivo began to laugh but kept his violin beneath his jacket.

Ada held out her hand.

For perhaps a minute, the old waiting room smelled of wet stone and leaves.

Then the cloud thinned until there was nothing left to watch.

Mara fetched towels.

Ada dried the table with the others. When they finished, she sat down heavily.

“Seventeen years,” she said.

Nobody tried to improve on that.

Later, she asked for a copy of the photograph from the acquisition file.

***

The council granted the museum another year.

It was not a victory anyone could frame. The funding was reduced, and Mara spent September learning to write grant applications.

She changed the cloud’s ledger entry from “restless” to “dispersed” and invited Ada back. Then she left the door open until closing time.
